description: Hey! I'm Pooja — math background, backend developer (Node.js / TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Docker). Building real-time astronaut health monitoring software with statistical anomaly detection, based on NASA-STD-3001 standards.
summary:
CrewWatch is a real-time health monitoring system for people isolated from medical professionals — astronauts on space missions and communities in remote areas where a doctor cannot reach in time.
The system monitors nine vital signs continuously, learns each person's individual normal using Welford's online algorithm, and fires alerts the moment something starts to change — using z-score anomaly detection, linear regression trend detection, and multi-vital combination detection. Every alert includes plain-English first aid guidance calibrated for the specific environment: astronauts are directed to mission control; village health workers are directed to the nearest clinic.
A single Docker command runs the full system. The dashboard updates live via WebSocket every five seconds, works offline via a service worker, and includes a symptom checker for people without medical devices, a simple-language mode for non-technical users, and a one-click health report export.
details:
CrewWatch monitors nine vital signs in real time: heart rate, blood oxygen (SpO₂), systolic and diastolic blood pressure, body temperature, respiration rate, radiation dose, sleep hours, and mood.

HOW IT WORKS

Most health tools compare readings against fixed population thresholds. CrewWatch instead learns each person's deviation in O(1) per reading. It then computes a z-score for every new reading: how many standard deviations is this from this specific person's normal? This catches problems that population thresholds miss entirely.

Three detection layers run on every reading:

1. Anomaly detection — z-score per vital with three severity levels (2.5 / 3.0 / 3.5 standard deviations)

2. Trend detection — least-squares linear regression over the last 20 readings per vital, catching slow

deterioration before it becomes a crisis

3. Combination detection — five dangerous multi-vital patterns (e.g. low SpO₂ + high heart rate = respiratory stress) that are more serious than either vital alone

A composite risk score (0–100) aggregates all active alerts and is broadcast to all connected dashboards via WebSocket on every reading event.

GUIDANCE ENGINE

Every alert carries two plain-English fields: a one-sentence description of what is happening, and step-by-step first aid guidance written for a non-medical person. Guidance is calibrated per vital, per direction (high vs. low), and per environment — astronauts receive space-specific escalation ("contact mission control or the flight

surgeon"); village users receive clinic-based escalation.

FEATURES FOR RESOURCE-LIMITED SETTINGS

- Symptom checker: 7-question modal for people without any medical devices

- Simple view: replaces all numbers with status words (Normal / Watch / Concern / Critical)

- Disaster mode: strips the UI to critical vitals only for mass-casualty scenarios

- Offline support: service worker caches the dashboard; works without internet

- PDF export: one-click health report with all active alerts and guidance text

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

TypeScript, Node.js 20, Express 5, PostgreSQL 16, WebSocket (ws), Chart.js, Docker, Docker Compose. No external cloud services — runs entirely on a local machine or any Linux server.

INTENDED IMPACT

The same codebase serves two populations that have never shared a health monitoring tool: astronauts on long-duration missions, and village health workers in areas without reliable medical infrastructure. The dual-environment design is intentional — the underlying health problem (early deterioration going undetected far from medical help) is identical in both contexts.
